title: Fox season on the Mornington Peninsula: when losses peak and what to do about it
desc: When foxes do the most damage on Peninsula hobby farms and horse properties, and how to time control so it actually works.
paras: Foxes are on the Peninsula all year, but the damage comes in two waves. The first is late winter into spring, when vixens are feeding cubs and lambs, kids and cria are on the ground. The second is autumn, when the year's cubs leave the den and go looking for easy food, which on the Peninsula usually means a chook run.

If you only control foxes once a year, do it in the four weeks before your first lambs or kids are due. A vixen with a den nearby will take a lamb a night, and a single night of thermal shooting before lambing removes the resident pair and often the den altogether.

Poultry losses are different. A fox that has found a chook run will come back every night until the run is empty or the fox is dead, so the right time to call is the night after the first loss. Lock the birds up, leave the run as it is, and we work the approach the fox has been using.

Baiting is rarely an option here. Most Peninsula blocks are too close to neighbours, dogs and public land for 1080 or PAPP, and the Shire's dog population makes it a real risk. Shooting is target-specific: every fox is identified through a thermal scope before a shot is taken.

One night is a start, not a finish. Foxes from neighbouring bush refill empty territory within weeks. We log every den we find with GPS and recommend a second visit three to six weeks after the first, then a monthly program through lambing for properties with a history of losses.

title: Deer in Peninsula vineyards: what the damage looks like and what the law allows
desc: Fallow and hog deer are now established around Red Hill, Main Ridge and Arthurs Seat. Here is what they cost growers and what a landholder can legally do.
paras: Ten years ago deer were a novelty on the Peninsula. Today fallow deer are established through Red Hill, Main Ridge and the Arthurs Seat hinterland, with hog deer along the Westernport bush and red deer appearing around Flinders. Growers see the evidence most mornings: broken trellis wire, stripped shoots at budburst, trampled netting and rubbed posts in autumn.

In Victoria, deer are unprotected on private land. That means a landholder can control them, or authorise someone to, without a permit from the state. The shooter still needs a firearms licence endorsed for the work, a Game Licence from the Game Management Authority, and the landholder's written authority. Properties close to houses or roads also need the shooter to hold a Victoria Police Public Place Permit.

Deer move between bush cover and feed at dawn and dusk, so control works best along the bush boundary at those times rather than in the vineyard rows. We plan shot positions with clear backstops at a daytime assessment, use thermal spotting to find animals in cover, and remove or dress carcasses on site depending on what the grower wants.

Where a property has steady deer numbers and the owner is happy with regular visits, control can often be done free of charge in exchange for harvesting. For most vineyards the practical arrangement is a monthly program from budburst through veraison, when the damage is concentrated.
Fencing still matters. Deer-proof fencing on the bush side of a vineyard is expensive, but combined with regular control it is the only approach that keeps a block clean season after season.

title: Why we don't bait: dogs, owls and 1080 on the Peninsula
desc: Baits kill more than foxes and rabbits. Why bait-free shooting is the right call on most Mornington Peninsula properties.
paras: Every year Peninsula vets treat dogs that have eaten fox baits, and wildlife carers pick up barn owls and powerful owls dying from rat bait. Baiting works in broadacre country where there is nothing else around to eat it. On five-acre blocks with neighbours, pets and bush reserves on every side, it mostly kills the wrong things.

1080 and PAPP fox baits are regulated for exactly that reason. On the Peninsula the distance rules from houses, roads and boundaries rule most properties out, and a dog that finds a bait usually dies before it reaches a vet.

Rat baits are the quieter problem. Anticoagulant baits in a stable or chook shed are eaten by rats that then die slowly in the open, where owls, kookaburras and the farm dog find them. Second-generation baits persist through the food chain. The barn owl hunting your paddocks at night is doing more rat control than the bait station ever will.

Shooting is the alternative that fits small properties. It is target-specific: with thermal optics every animal is identified before a shot is taken, and nothing is left in the paddock or shed afterwards. Small-calibre rifles and careful shot placement keep disturbance low.

Where shooting alone is not enough, for a big rabbit warren system say, we map the warrens so they can be ripped or fumigated, which deals with the problem at its source without leaving poison lying around.
